case_prompt:
A 25-year-old man with no prior medical history presented 3 days after the sudden onset of involuntary motor tics and vocalizations. He initially developed facial twitches and left-sided winking up to 12 times per minute, followed by whistling sounds. He denied initial stressors but later disclosed a marital separation four months earlier, his daughter’s move out of the home, and that he had entered his daughter’s room—his first return since the separation—one week before tic onset. He also noted a former coworker with Tourette’s syndrome.

Review of systems was otherwise negative. On examination, vital signs were normal. Neurologic evaluation showed intact cranial nerves II–XII, full symmetric strength, normal reflexes, sensation, coordination, and gait. During the exam, he exhibited frequent involuntary facial movements, left-sided hemifacial spasms, blinking, grimacing, clicking, and whistling. Psychiatric assessment revealed clear and fluent speech without suicidal or homicidal ideation. On further probing he endorsed increased jumpiness, decreased sleep, persistent ruminations, and an impending court date for alleged domestic abuse. His Patient Health Questionnaire-9 score was 4 and his Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 score was 15.

diagnostic_reasoning: 1. Tourette’s syndrome was considered because of the co-occurrence of motor and vocal tics — “Differential diagnosis included Tourette's syndrome, dystonia, Parkinsonism, Wilson disease, enhanced physiologic tremor, Multiple sclerosis.” 2. Dystonia was considered given the abnormal involuntary movements — “Differential diagnosis included Tourette's syndrome, dystonia, Parkinsonism, Wilson disease, enhanced physiologic tremor, Multiple sclerosis.” 3. Parkinsonism was considered as movement disorders can present with tremor or bradykinesia — “Differential diagnosis included Tourette's syndrome, dystonia, Parkinsonism, Wilson disease, enhanced physiologic tremor, Multiple sclerosis.” 4. Wilson disease was considered because it can manifest with movement abnormalities — “Differential diagnosis included Tourette's syndrome, dystonia, Parkinsonism, Wilson disease, enhanced physiologic tremor, Multiple sclerosis.” 5. Enhanced physiologic tremor was considered for its tremulous component — “Differential diagnosis included Tourette's syndrome, dystonia, Parkinsonism, Wilson disease, enhanced physiologic tremor, Multiple sclerosis.” 6. Multiple sclerosis was considered as a demyelinating cause of motor symptoms — “Differential diagnosis included Tourette's syndrome, dystonia, Parkinsonism, Wilson disease, enhanced physiologic tremor, Multiple sclerosis.” 7. Organic causes were excluded by the absence of neurologic abnormalities on examination, obviating further testing — “Due to high suspicion of psychogenic movement disorder with very reassuring neurologic physical examination, no follow‐on labs, radiology, or special testing was required to begin treatment.” 8. Psychogenic movement disorder was identified based on sudden onset, stress triggers, suggestibility, and a normal exam — “Basis for diagnosis takes into account a normal physical exam with multiple typical characteristics of PMD that includes, but is not limited to: sudden abrupt onset of symptoms, Movements triggered or worsened by emotional or physical stressors, cessation of movements may occur by trialing a suggested physical treatment…”

selection.screen_reason: Abrupt adult-onset tics after major stressors with a normal neurological exam and high anxiety; a history-driven functional movement disorder.
selection.second_look_note: Abrupt adult-onset tics after stressors that the patient discloses on probing, with a normal neurological exam, make this a history-driven diagnosis.
